Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses brief exposition at the beginning to establish the setting (the flooding city) and the narrator's aimless state of mind, and uses summary at the end to compress the passage of time after the flood ("The rescue boats came through sometime after midnight," "I have walked past the building many times since"). Between these points, the story relies on vivid, real-time scenes—such as the encounter with the burned chair on the curb and the prolonged, eerie observation outside the couple's window as the water rises—to build tension and bring the surreal narrative to life. This balance keeps the pacing steady and the reader fully engaged.
